title: Celsus on serving more than one master
source_text: Ἐπηπόρησε δὲ ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων πρὸς ἡμᾶς. διὰ τί δαίμονας οὐ θεραπεύομεν· καὶ πρὸς ἃ εἶπε περὶ δαιμόνων ἀπηντήσαμεν κατὰ τὸ φαινόμενον ἡμῖν βούλημα τοῦ θείου λόγου. εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς ἐκείνοις ἡμᾶς εἰσάγει λέγοντας πρὸς τὴν ἐπαπόρησιν αὐτοῦ. θέλοντος ἡμᾶς καὶ τοὺς δαίμονας θεραπεύειν, ὅτι οὐχ οἷόν τε „δουλεύειν“ τὸν αὐτὸν πλείοσι „κυρίοις.“ τοῦτο δ᾿, ὡς οἴεται, στάσεως εἶναι φωνὴν τῶν, ὡς αὐτὸς ὠνόμασεν, ἀποτειχιζόντων ἑαυτοὺς καὶ ἀποῤῥηγνύντων ἀπὸ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀνθρώπων. νομίζει δὲ τοὺς τοῦτο λέγοντας τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς ἀπομάττεσθαι τὸ σφέτερον πάθος εἰς τὸν θεόν. διὸ καὶ ἐπὶ μὲν ἀνθρώπων χώραν ἔχειν οἴεται τὸν δουλεύοντά τινι μὴ ἂν εὐλόγως καὶ ἄλλῳ „δουλεύειν“ ἀνθρώπῳ, ὡς βλαπτομένου τοῦ ἑτέρου ἀπὸ τῆς διαφόρου δουλείας, μηδὲ τὸν φθάσαντα συνομωμοκέναι τινὶ συνομνύειν καὶ ἑτέρῳ ὡς βλάπτοντα, (καὶ) λόγον ἔχειν τὸ μὴ δουλεύειν ἅμα διαφόροις ἥρωσι καὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις δαίμοσιν· ἐπὶ δὲ θεοῦ, πρὸς ὃν οὔτε βλάβη τις οὔτε λύπη φθάνει, ἄλογον νομίζει τὸ φυλάττεσθαι ὁμοίως τοῖς περὶ ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἡρώων καὶ τοιῶνδε δαιμόνων θεραπεύειν θεοὺς πλείονας. φησὶ δὲ καὶ τὸν θεραπεύοντα θεοὺς πλείονας τῷ ἕν τι τῶν τοῦ μεγάλου θεραπεύειν φίλον καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ἐκείνῳ ποιεῖν καὶ προστίθησιν ὅτι οὐδ᾿ ἔξεστι τιμᾶσθαί τινι ᾧ μὴ ἐξ ἐκείνου τοῦτο δέδοται. διότι τιμῶν τις καὶ σέβων, φησὶ, τοὺς ἐκείνου πάντας οὐ λυπεῖ τὸν θεὸν, οὗ πάντες εἰσίν.
pass_a_gloss: He raised a further difficulty (ἐπαπορέω) in the things before these against us: why we do not worship (θεραπεύω) demons (δαίμων); and to what he said about demons we answered according to the intent (βούλημα) of the divine word (θεῖος λόγος) appearing to us. Then next to those he introduces (εἰσάγω) us saying, toward his difficulty (ἐπαπόρησις), as he wishes us to worship also the demons, that it is not possible for the same man to 'serve' (δουλεύω) more 'lords' (κύριος). This, as he supposes, is the voice (φωνή) of sedition (στάσις) of those who, as he himself named, wall themselves off (ἀποτειχίζω) and break themselves away (ἀπορρήγνυμι) from the rest of men. He thinks those saying this, as far as in them, wipe/stamp off (ἀπομάσσομαι) their own passion (πάθος) onto God. Therefore he thinks it has place among men that the one serving someone would not reasonably (εὐλόγως) also serve another man, as the other being harmed (βλάπτω) by the different service (δουλεία); nor the one who has already sworn together (συνόμνυμι) with someone to swear together also with another as harming; and it has reason (λόγον ἔχειν) not to serve at once different heroes (ἥρως) and such demons; but in the case of God, toward whom neither any harm (βλάβη) nor grief (λύπη) arrives, he thinks it unreasonable (ἄλογον) to guard against (φυλάττομαι), like the things about men and heroes and such demons, worshipping more gods. He says also that the one worshipping more gods, by worshipping some one of the things of the great [God], does in this also what is dear (φίλον) to him; and he adds that it is not permitted (ἔξεστι) for anyone to be honoured (τιμάω) to whom this has not been given from him. Wherefore one honouring and revering (σέβω), he says, all his does not grieve (λυπέω) God, whose all are.
pass_b_english: In what came before, he raised the question against us why we do not worship demons; and we answered what he said about demons according to what seemed to us the intent of the divine word. Then, next after that, he brings us in as saying, in answer to his question, since he wants us to worship the demons too, that the same man cannot “serve” several “masters” (Matthew 6:24). This, he thinks, is the voice of sedition, the voice of those who, as he himself called them, “wall themselves off and break away from the rest of mankind.” He supposes that those who say this are, as far as in them lies, projecting their own passion onto God.

That is why he thinks it holds good among men that one who serves someone could not reasonably “serve” another man too, since one of the two would be harmed by the divided service; and that one who has already sworn alliance with someone should not swear alliance with another as well, since that would harm the first; and that it is reasonable not to serve at the same time various heroes and demons of that kind. But in the case of God, whom neither harm nor grief can reach, he thinks it unreasonable to guard against worshipping several gods, as one does in matters concerning men and heroes and demons of this kind. He also says that the one who worships several gods, by worshipping some one of the beings that belong to the great God, in this too does what is dear to Him; and he adds that no one may be honoured to whom this has not been given by Him. “Therefore,” he says, “one who honours and reverences all who are His does not grieve God, to whom they all belong.”

choices.choice: Origen refers back to Book 7 (from about 7.62), where Celsus asked why Christians do not worship demons. ‘serve ... masters’ is the language of Matthew 6:24 (also Luke 16:13), marked as quoted words in Koetschau; Origen quotes the saying in full in 8.3. The phrase ‘wall themselves off and break away’ is put in quotation marks because Origen says Celsus ‘himself named’ them so; the rest of Celsus’s argument is reported in indirect speech and kept indirect, except for the final sentence, which is framed with φησί and given as direct quotation. ἀπομάττεσθαι τὸ σφέτερον πάθος εἰς τὸν θεόν: ‘stamp (as an impression) their own passion upon God’, i.e., attribute human jealousy to God. (καὶ) before λόγον ἔχειν is Koetschau’s supplement, accepted. τῶν τοῦ μεγάλου: neuter or masculine plural, ‘the beings that belong to the great God’; ‘God’ is supplied from context (θεόν at the sentence end). διότι introducing Celsus’s last sentence is taken as inferential (‘Therefore’), as the sense requires. ὡς βλαπτομένου τοῦ ἑτέρου: ‘since one of the two would be harmed’ (ἕτερος, one of a pair).
